questions.question: What is try-with-resources in Java and why was it introduced?
questions.title: Try-With-Resources in Java Explained
questions.direct_answer: Try-with-resources is a Java 7 language feature that closes each successfully initialized `AutoCloseable` resource as the statement exits, in reverse declaration order. It replaces error-prone manual cleanup. If both the body and closing fail, the body failure stays primary and close failures are suppressed; if only closing fails, that close failure propagates.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know try-with-resources auto-closes AutoCloseable resources and why it replaced manual finally-close
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Still writing manual finally blocks to close resources, or not null-checking before close in the old pattern
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention it also fixes the suppressed-exception problem: a failure in close() no longer hides the original try exception

sections.title: What try-with-resources Is
sections.content:
Try-with-resources puts resources in the `try (...)` header and applies Java's automatic closing rules when the statement exits. A resource must implement `AutoCloseable`. Successfully initialized resources close in reverse declaration order, whether the body completes normally or abruptly.

The feature avoids common manual cleanup mistakes: forgetting a close on one path, closing dependent resources in the wrong order, or replacing the body failure with a cleanup failure. When the body is already throwing, close failures are attached as suppressed exceptions. If the body succeeded and a close fails, that close failure is the primary exception.

A resource declared in the header cannot be reassigned. Since Java 9, an existing final or effectively final local variable can also be named in the resource list. Automatic closing is structured language behavior; it does not protect against process termination or a `close()` implementation that hangs.

sections.title: try-with-resources at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Declare in header|~try (Resource r = ...)|since Java 7|r must be AutoCloseable|scoped to the block
blue|Auto-close|~close() called for you|on normal exit|and on exception|no finally needed
amber|Reverse order|~Last opened, first closed|like a stack|matches dependencies|safe teardown
rose|Suppressed exceptions|~close() failure recorded|original still propagates|getSuppressed() to see them|no lost errors

sections.title: How try-with-resources Runs
sections.content:
Follow the structured-exit rules for a successfully initialized resource.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Initialize resource in try header"] --> B["Run try body"]
    B --> C{"Body throws?"}
    C -->|No| D["Call close() while exiting"]
    C -->|Yes| E["Call close() while exception is pending"]
    E --> F{"close() also throws?"}
    F -->|No| G["Body exception propagates"]
    F -->|Yes| H["Attach close failure as suppressed"]
    D --> I["Normal exit unless close throws"]
```

This covers structured control leaving the statement. It cannot promise cleanup after process termination, and a faulty `close()` can still hang or fail.

sections.title: Without try-with-resources: fragile manual close
With try-with-resources: automatically closed on structured exit
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Still writing manual `finally` close** when try-with-resources would be simpler and safer.
- **Forgetting the resource must implement `AutoCloseable`** — otherwise it won't compile in the header.
- **Assuming close order is declaration order** — it's *reverse*.
- **Reassigning the resource variable** — try-with-resources resources are effectively final.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Resource type:** must implement `AutoCloseable`.
- **Close order:** reverse order for every successfully initialized resource.
- **Body plus close fail:** body exception remains primary; close failures are suppressed.
- **Only close fails:** close failure propagates as primary.
- **Variables:** header declarations are final; Java 9+ can reuse final/effectively final locals.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Try-with-resources automatically closes successfully initialized AutoCloseable resources as the statement exits. Resources close in reverse declaration order, which is useful when later resources depend on earlier ones. It replaced verbose manual finally cleanup and handles competing failures correctly.

If the body and close both throw, the body exception remains primary and close failures are available through `getSuppressed`. If only close throws, that close exception propagates. Resource declarations in the header cannot be reassigned, and since Java 9 an existing final or effectively final local may be used in the resource list.

beats.text: Try-with-resources is a Java 7 feature. It automatically closes anything that implements `AutoCloseable`. You declare the resource inside the `try` parentheses. When the block exits, Java calls its close method for you. It works whether the block finishes normally or throws.

The old try-finally pattern was easy to get wrong. You'd forget the null check, or forget to close at all. Worse, if close threw, it hid the real exception. Try-with-resources fixes all three. It's shorter, and it can't leak.

Many resources close in reverse order of declaration, last opened first.
If the body is already failing, its exception remains primary and a close failure is suppressed; if only close fails, the close failure is primary.

questions.question: What is AutoCloseable and how does it relate to try-with-resources?
questions.title: AutoCloseable Interface and Try-With-Resources
questions.direct_answer: `AutoCloseable` declares `void close() throws Exception`; an object assignable to it can be managed by try-with-resources. `Closeable` extends it and narrows the declared failure to `IOException`. AutoCloseable does not require `close()` to be idempotent, although idempotence is often a useful class-specific design; callers must follow the resource's documented lifecycle.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know AutoCloseable is the contract behind try-with-resources and can implement it on a custom class
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Closeable and AutoCloseable, or thinking only JDK classes can be used in try-with-resources
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note Closeable extends AutoCloseable and predates it (Java 5 vs 7), and that repeated-close behavior should follow the concrete contract

sections.title: The Contract Behind try-with-resources
sections.content:
`AutoCloseable` is the interface recognized by try-with-resources. It declares `void close() throws Exception`. A resource expression whose type is assignable to `AutoCloseable` can appear in the resource list, and Java applies automatic close calls on exit.

`java.io.Closeable` extends `AutoCloseable` and narrows `close()` to `IOException`. Closeable's contract requires a second close to have no effect, while the broader AutoCloseable contract does **not** require idempotence. An AutoCloseable implementation should therefore document what repeated close means; making it idempotent is often helpful but not a language rule.

An implementation may narrow the declared exception or throw no checked exception. It should release only resources it owns and preserve meaningful failure information.

sections.title: AutoCloseable vs Closeable
sections.content:
emerald|AutoCloseable|~Root resource contract|close() throws Exception|enables try-with-resources|idempotence not required
blue|Closeable|~I/O subinterface|extends AutoCloseable|close() throws IOException|repeated close has no effect
amber|Implementation|~May narrow or omit checked throw|release owned resources|document repeated close|preserve useful failures
rose|Direction|~Closeable is AutoCloseable|reverse is not guaranteed|use assignability in try header|read concrete contract

sections.title: How the Interfaces Relate
sections.content:
Read the arrows as is-a: `Closeable` is an `AutoCloseable`, never the reverse. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["AutoCloseable
close() throws Exception"] --> B["Closeable
close() throws IOException"] A --> C["Your custom class
implements AutoCloseable"] B --> D["BufferedReader, InputStream"] A --> E["JDBC: Connection, Statement, ResultSet"] ``` Everything under `AutoCloseable` works in a try-with-resources header — JDK types and your own classes alike.

sections.title: A Custom AutoCloseable Resource
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing the direction:** `Closeable` extends `AutoCloseable`, not the other way around.
- **Thinking only JDK resources qualify:** any assignable implementation can appear in the resource list.
- **Assuming every `close()` is idempotent:** `Closeable` requires harmless repeat close, while `AutoCloseable` does not.
- **Calling close manually inside the try:** this can cause a second close with implementation-specific behavior.
- **Declaring `throws Exception` unnecessarily:** an implementation may narrow the checked type or declare none.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **AutoCloseable:** `void close() throws Exception`.
- **Try-with-resources:** accepts resources assignable to AutoCloseable.
- **Closeable:** I/O subinterface; narrows to `IOException`.
- **Idempotence:** required by Closeable's close contract, not by AutoCloseable in general.
- **Implementation:** may narrow the exception or declare none.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`AutoCloseable` is the contract used by try-with-resources. It declares `close()`, which may throw `Exception`. `Closeable` is an I/O-focused subinterface that narrows the declared failure to `IOException` and specifies that closing an already closed stream has no effect. `AutoCloseable` itself does not require repeated close calls to be harmless, although an implementation may make them so.

For example, `try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) { ... }` works because the reader is `Closeable`, and Java calls `reader.close()` when the block ends whether the body completes normally or throws. A database transaction scope could implement `AutoCloseable` with a different checked-failure contract. I therefore program to the documented lifecycle of the concrete resource and let its `close()` method declare a narrower exception when possible.

questions.question: Can try-with-resources be used without a catch block?
questions.title: Try-With-Resources Without Catch Block
questions.direct_answer: Yes. try-with-resources can stand alone with **no `catch` and no `finally`** — `try (Resource r = ...) { ... }` is valid. The resource is still auto-closed, and any exception simply **propagates to the caller**. You add a `catch` only if you actually want to handle the exception here; otherwise the bare form is perfectly fine.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know try-with-resources is itself a complete statement that doesn't require catch or finally
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking you must add a catch (or finally) when using try-with-resources
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify that the implicit close acts like a finally, so adding an explicit finally is usually redundant

sections.title: try-with-resources Is Complete on Its Own
sections.content:
**Yes — a try-with-resources can stand alone**, with no `catch` and no `finally`. So `try (Resource r = open()) { use(r); }` compiles and runs fine on its own.

Why it works: normally a `try` needs a `catch` or a `finally`. But **try-with-resources counts as that required clause** — the resource declaration carries an implicit close that behaves like a `finally`.

**What happens on the way out:** the resource is closed automatically, and if anything throws, the exception **propagates to the caller** unhandled. Closing and exception handling are two separate jobs.

- **Bare form** — `try(r) { ... }`, exception propagates
- **With `catch`** — handle the error here when you can recover
- **With `finally`** — only for extra cleanup beyond closing

> **Key rule:** if the propagating exception is checked (like `IOException`), your method must declare `throws` — the implicit close doesn't change that.

sections.title: Forms of try-with-resources
sections.content:
emerald|Bare form|~No catch, no finally|try (r = ...) { ... }|valid & common|exception propagates
blue|With catch|~Handle here|try (r=...) {..} catch {..}|when you can recover|close still happens first
amber|With finally|~Usually redundant|close is automatic|finally for extra cleanup only|rarely needed
rose|Implicit close|~Acts like finally|satisfies the try rule|runs before catch|reverse order if multiple

sections.title: Catch Is Optional, Close Is Not
sections.content:
The decision is only about who handles the error — the close runs either way.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["try (resource) { ... }"] --> B["Block exits, JVM closes the resource"]
    B --> C{"Did the body throw?"}
    C -->|No| D["Method returns normally"]
    C -->|Yes| E{"Is there a catch here?"}
    E -->|Yes| F["Handle it locally"]
    E -->|No| G["Exception propagates to caller"]
```

Notice the close in step two happens before the catch decision — handling is a separate concern.

sections.title: Standalone try-with-resources (no catch)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking a `catch` is mandatory.** The implicit close satisfies the `try` requirement.
- **Adding a redundant `finally` to close** — try-with-resources already closes for you.
- **Forgetting to declare/propagate the checked exception** when there's no `catch` (`throws IOException`).
- **Swallowing with an empty `catch`** just to avoid declaring `throws` — let it propagate instead.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Bare try-with-resources is valid** — no `catch`, no `finally` required.
- **The implicit close acts as the `finally`**, satisfying the language rule.
- **Unhandled exceptions propagate** to the caller (declare `throws` if checked).
- **Add `catch` only to handle** the exception locally.
- **An explicit `finally` is usually redundant** for closing resources.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Yes, you can use try-with-resources completely on its own, with no catch block and no finally block. Normally the rule is that a plain try has to be followed by a catch or a finally, but with try-with-resources, the resource declaration itself satisfies that requirement, because it carries an implicit close that behaves just like a finally. So writing try, open your resource in the parentheses, use it in the body, and then nothing after the closing brace — that compiles and runs perfectly. When the block exits, the resource's close method is called automatically, and if an exception was thrown, it just propagates up to the caller unhandled. The one thing you need to remember is that if the exception is checked, like an I O exception, and you're not catching it, then your method has to declare it with throws, because you're passing the responsibility up the chain. You only add a catch block when you genuinely want to handle the error at this level — for instance, to log it and return a default value. And adding an explicit finally is allowed, but for the purpose of closing the resource it's redundant, because that's exactly what try-with-resources is already doing for you. The only reason you'd add a finally is if you have some additional cleanup beyond closing the declared resources. A mistake I'd avoid is adding an empty catch block just to dodge declaring throws, because that swallows the exception and hides problems. If you can't handle it meaningfully, it's better to let it propagate.

questions.question: Can you declare multiple resources in a try-with-resources statement?
questions.title: Multiple Resources in Try-With-Resources
questions.direct_answer: Yes. Separate resources with semicolons. Initializers run left to right, and every successfully initialized resource is closed in reverse order. If a later initializer fails, earlier resources are still closed. If the body succeeds but several closes fail, the first close failure is primary and later close failures are suppressed; if the body fails, close failures are suppressed under the body failure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know multiple resources are semicolon-separated and closed in reverse declaration order
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using commas instead of semicolons, or assuming close order matches declaration order
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why reverse order matters when one resource depends on another (e.g., ResultSet before Statement before Connection)

sections.title: Several Resources, Closed in Reverse
sections.content:
A try-with-resources statement may declare several resources separated by semicolons. Initializers run from left to right. Every resource that finishes initialization is then eligible for automatic closing in the reverse order. If initialization of a later resource fails, Java still closes the earlier successfully initialized resources.

Reverse order matches dependencies such as `Connection`, then `PreparedStatement`, then `ResultSet`: the result set closes before the statement and connection. Java attempts the remaining close operations even if one close throws.

Exception priority depends on what failed first. A body exception remains primary and close failures are suppressed. If the body succeeded, the first close failure in reverse-close order becomes primary and further close failures are suppressed under it. 'A close failure is suppressed' is therefore not universally true.

sections.title: Multiple Resources Rules
sections.content:
emerald|Semicolon-separated|~Not commas|try (A a=..; B b=..)|any count allowed|each is closed
amber|Reverse close order|~Last opened, first closed|like a stack|safe for dependencies|automatic
blue|JDBC example|~ResultSet -> Statement -> Connection|child before parent|avoids 'closed' errors|natural unwind
rose|All still close|~Even if one throws|remaining closes run|failure priority follows primary/suppressed rules|remaining close calls are attempted

sections.title: Open Left-to-Right, Close Right-to-Left
sections.content:
Resources unwind like a stack — the order is automatic and dependency-safe.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Open A"] --> B["Open B"]
    B --> C["Open C"]
    C --> D["Run the try body"]
    D --> E["close() on C"]
    E --> F["close() on B"]
    F --> G["close() on A"]
```

The last resource opened (C) is the first one closed — child before parent.

sections.title: Declaring and Closing Multiple Resources
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using commas instead of semicolons** between resources — won't compile.
- **Assuming declaration order = close order.** It's the *reverse*.
- **Manually closing in the wrong order** in legacy code — leads to 'connection already closed' errors.
- **Cramming unrelated resources** into one header when separate try blocks would read clearer.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Syntax:** separate resources with semicolons.
- **Initialize:** left to right.
- **Close:** every successfully initialized resource, right to left.
- **Initializer failure:** earlier initialized resources still close.
- **Failure priority:** body first if it failed; otherwise first close failure is primary and later ones are suppressed.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Multiple resources are separated with semicolons. Their initializers run left to right and every successfully initialized resource closes in reverse order. If a later initializer fails, the earlier resources still close. Java also continues attempting the remaining closes after one close fails.

If the body already failed, close failures are suppressed under that body exception. If the body succeeded, the first close failure becomes primary and later close failures are suppressed under it. That distinction is important when reading a trace.

questions.question: How does try-with-resources work with JDBC — Connection, Statement, and ResultSet?
questions.title: Try-With-Resources with JDBC
questions.direct_answer: JDBC `Connection`, `Statement`/`PreparedStatement`, and `ResultSet` implement `AutoCloseable`, so try-with-resources closes successfully opened objects in reverse order. Closing a pooled `Connection` normally returns it to the pool rather than physically closing the database session. PreparedStatement bind parameters protect data values from SQL injection when used correctly, but SQL identifiers and dynamically built clauses need separate safe handling.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can apply try-with-resources to the real JDBC trio and know why leaking connections is catastrophic
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Closing only the Connection (not Statement/ResultSet), or building queries with string concatenation instead of PreparedStatement
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that leaked connections exhaust the pool and take the whole service down, and that PreparedStatement also prevents value-based SQL injection when placeholders are used correctly

sections.title: JDBC Is the Textbook Case for try-with-resources
sections.content:
JDBC's `Connection`, `Statement`/`PreparedStatement`, and `ResultSet` implement `AutoCloseable`. Declare them in dependency order and Java closes successfully opened resources in reverse: result set, statement, then connection. If creation of the statement or result set fails, resources already opened are still closed.

With a connection pool, calling `Connection.close()` normally returns the logical connection to the pool; it does not necessarily close the physical database connection. Pools may be fixed, elastic within limits, or configured differently, but leaked logical connections can still exhaust the available capacity and delay or fail requests. Try-with-resources greatly reduces that risk; it does not make leaks impossible if code transfers ownership or a driver misbehaves.

Use `PreparedStatement` placeholders for **data values** instead of concatenating untrusted values into SQL. Placeholders generally cannot represent table names, column names, or arbitrary SQL syntax, so dynamic identifiers need allow-lists or a safe query builder. Statement reuse and caching depend on the driver and pool, not only on choosing PreparedStatement.

sections.title: The JDBC Trio
sections.content:
blue|Connection|~Pool slot, scarce|implements AutoCloseable|leaking exhausts the pool|closed LAST
emerald|PreparedStatement|~Parameterized query|implements AutoCloseable|prevents value-based SQL injection when placeholders are used correctly|closed second
amber|ResultSet|~Query rows cursor|implements AutoCloseable|tied to its statement|closed FIRST
rose|The leak|~Forgotten close()|pool runs dry|requests block / time out|service outage

sections.title: Why a Leaked Connection Kills the Service
sections.content:
Each un-closed `ResultSet` pins its statement, which pins its connection — and the pool drains.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Request opens a Connection"] --> B["Query runs, ResultSet not closed"]
    B --> C["ResultSet pins Statement pins Connection"]
    C --> D["Pool slot never returned"]
    D --> E{"Pool exhausted?"}
    E -->|No| A
    E -->|Yes| F["New requests block, service stalls"]
```

try-with-resources breaks this loop: all three close in the right order on every path.

sections.title: Wrong: string-built query + manual close that leaks
Right: try-with-resources + PreparedStatement
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Closing only the `Connection`.** The `Statement` and `ResultSet` leak too — declare all three.
- **String-concatenating SQL.** Use `PreparedStatement` with `?` parameters to stop SQL injection.
- **Leaking on the error path.** Manual code that closes only on success still leaks when a query throws.
- **Holding the connection too long.** Open late, close early; don't span unrelated work.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **AutoCloseable JDBC types:** Connection, Statement/PreparedStatement, and ResultSet.
- **Reverse close:** ResultSet, statement, connection.
- **Pool meaning:** Connection.close normally returns a logical connection to its pool.
- **Leak impact:** can exhaust configured capacity and delay or fail work.
- **SQL safety:** bind untrusted values; allow-list or safely build dynamic identifiers separately.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
JDBC resources implement AutoCloseable, so I declare the connection, prepared statement, and result set in dependency order and let try-with-resources close them in reverse. Successfully opened resources also close if a later initializer or the query fails.

For a pooled connection, close normally returns the logical connection to the pool instead of tearing down the physical session. That is essential because leaked connections can consume the pool's configured capacity. I use PreparedStatement placeholders for untrusted data values. They do not parameterize table or column names, so dynamic SQL structure requires a separate allow-list or safe builder.

Connection and PreparedStatement in DAO code

speakable_v2.hook: One forgotten `ResultSet` close can drain your connection pool and take the whole service down. Here's the JDBC pattern that stops it.

beats.text: In JDBC the `Connection`, `Statement` and `ResultSet` all implement AutoCloseable. Try-with-resources then automatically closes anything that implements AutoCloseable when the block exits. So declare the trio in the header and skip every manual close.

JDBC resources are expensive. A `Connection` is a slot in a small, fixed pool. Forget to close even one per request, and the pool slowly drains. Once it's empty, every new request just blocks, and the service stalls.

items: Declare the Connection and PreparedStatement in the outer try header.
Put the ResultSet in an inner try, since it has a shorter life.
They close in reverse: ResultSet first, then the statement, then the connection.
If a query throws, Java still closes all of them, so the pool stays healthy.

beats.text: Picture a Java 17 REST service doing a hundred reads a second. Skip the closes, and a small pool runs dry in seconds. Here's the non-obvious part. Each open `ResultSet` pins its statement, which pins its connection. Try-with-resources closes all three in the right order, so this just can't happen.

items: Closing only the Connection. The Statement and ResultSet leak too.
Building SQL with string concatenation. Use a PreparedStatement with bind parameters.
Holding the connection during unrelated work. Open it late and close it early.

speakable_v2.cap: Wrap every JDBC resource in try-with-resources. It's the only reliable way to keep connections from leaking and the pool alive.

questions.question: What are suppressed exceptions in try-with-resources?
questions.title: Suppressed Exceptions in Try-With-Resources
questions.direct_answer: When the try body throws and closing also throws, the body exception remains primary and each close failure is attached through `addSuppressed`; callers inspect them with `getSuppressed()`. If the body succeeds, the first close failure is primary and later close failures are suppressed. A naive manual finally can replace an earlier failure, but careful manual code can preserve it too.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand which exception is primary when both the body and close() throw, and how to retrieve the other
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the close() exception wins (as in manual finally) and that the original is lost
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast with manual try-finally where the close exception masked the real one, and mention addSuppressed/getSuppressed

sections.title: When Both the Body and close() Fail
sections.content:
A suppressed exception is a secondary failure attached to the exception that Java chooses as primary during try-with-resources cleanup.

If the body throws, that body exception remains primary. Any resource close failures are attached to it and appear under `Suppressed:` in a formatted trace. `getSuppressed()` returns those secondary Throwables.

If the body completes normally but closing fails, the first close failure in reverse close order becomes primary. If additional resources also fail to close, those later failures are suppressed under the first. Thus, a close exception is not always suppressed.

The feature improves on a **naive** `finally` block where `close()` throws and replaces a pending body exception. Carefully written manual cleanup could preserve both, but try-with-resources applies the correct pattern consistently.

sections.title: Suppressed Exceptions Explained
sections.content:
emerald|Primary exception|~From the try body|the real cause|propagates to caller|kept intact
amber|Suppressed exception|~From close()|attached, not lost|getSuppressed() to read|shown as 'Suppressed:' in trace
rose|Old finally pattern|~close() exception won|original replaced|real cause hidden|why try-with-resources is better
blue|API|~addSuppressed / getSuppressed|on Throwable|JVM wires it up|you rarely call them directly

sections.title: Which Exception Reaches the Caller
sections.content:
Both errors survive — one as primary, one attached underneath it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["try body throws (primary)"] --> B["Java calls close()"]
    B --> C{"close() throws too?"}
    C -->|No| D["Primary propagates alone"]
    C -->|Yes| E["close failure added via addSuppressed()"]
    E --> F["Primary propagates to caller"]
    F --> G["getSuppressed() reveals the close failure"]
```

When the body has thrown, that body exception remains primary; the close failure rides along.

sections.title: Primary vs Suppressed in Action
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming the `close()` exception wins.** In try-with-resources, the *body* exception is primary.
- **Forgetting `getSuppressed()` exists.** The close failure is still recorded — go read it.
- **Replicating the old `finally` bug** by manually closing and rethrowing in a way that drops the original.
- **Ignoring 'Suppressed:' lines** in a stack trace — they often explain a secondary cleanup failure.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Body fails first:** body exception is primary; close failures are suppressed.
- **Body succeeds:** first close failure is primary.
- **More close failures:** attached as suppressed to the primary.
- **Read them:** call `getSuppressed()` or inspect `Suppressed:` trace lines.
- **Comparison:** naive manual finally may mask the body failure; careful code need not.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Suppressed exceptions preserve secondary cleanup failures. When the try body throws, its exception stays primary and failures from closing resources are attached to it. If the body succeeds, the first close failure becomes primary and later close failures are suppressed under it.

I inspect them with getSuppressed or the Suppressed lines in a trace. This avoids the common naive-finally bug where a close exception replaces the body exception, although manual code could preserve both if written carefully.

speakable_v2.hook: Two errors fire at once, one from your code and one from close. Which one reaches the caller? Try-with-resources flipped the old answer.

beats.text: A suppressed exception shows up when your `try` body throws and close throws too. Try-with-resources suppresses close-time exceptions into the primary one. So the body error stays primary and propagates. The close failure rides along, reachable later.

The old try-finally had a nasty bug. If both the body and finally threw, the finally error replaced the original. You lost the real cause. Try-with-resources fixes that, so the body error always wins.

items: The primary exception comes from the try body. That's the one you catch.
The suppressed exception comes from close. It attaches to the primary.
Call getSuppressed on the primary to read the close failures.
With several resources, each failing close adds its own suppressed entry.

beats.text: Picture a faulty resource in a Java 17 app. The body throws a work error, then close throws a cleanup error. Here's the non-obvious part. You catch the work error as primary, and the cleanup error sits inside getSuppressed. the primary and suppressed failures remain distinguishable.

items: Assuming the close error wins. The body error stays primary instead.
Forgetting getSuppressed exists, so you miss the recorded cleanup failure.
Recreating the old finally bug by closing and rethrowing in a way that drops the original.

speakable_v2.cap: Suppressed exceptions keep both errors visible, the real cause and the cleanup failure. That's a big win over the old finally, which silently lost the original.
